title: Maximize Consecutive Elements in an Array After Modification
statement:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers. First, you may raise any of its elements by 1 (each element at most once, and only by 1; you can also leave it unchanged). Then you choose one or more elements of the resulting array whose values, once sorted, form a run of consecutive integers with no gaps and no repeats: `[3, 4, 5]` qualifies, while `[3, 4, 6]` and `[1, 1, 2, 3]` do not.

Return the largest number of elements you can choose.
notes:
## Intuition

Since the chosen values must be distinct and consecutive, the answer is the longest chain `v, v + 1, v + 2, ...` in which each value comes from a different element, either kept or raised by one. Trying every raise choice is exponential. Instead, sort the array and build the chains left to right: an element with value `num` can extend a chain ending at `num - 1` (kept as `num`) or a chain ending at `num` (raised to `num + 1`). Every element in such a chain is no larger than `num`, so after sorting those chains are already known when `num` arrives.

## Approach

1. Sort `nums` in increasing order.
2. Let `dp` map a value `v` to the longest chain found so far whose largest value is `v`.
3. For each `num`, compute `raised = dp[num] + 1` (using `num + 1`) and `kept = dp[num - 1] + 1` (using `num`), both read before `dp` changes, so the element is not used twice.
4. Store the better of each with what `dp[num + 1]` and `dp[num]` already hold, and keep the overall maximum in `best`.
5. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted `nums` is `[1, 1, 1, 2, 5]`.

- First `1`: `raised = 1`, `kept = 1`, so `dp = {2: 1, 1: 1}`.
- Second `1`: `raised = dp[1] + 1 = 2`, `kept = 1`, so `dp[2] = 2`.
- Third `1`: the same values; nothing improves.
- `2`: `raised = dp[2] + 1 = 3` (chain 1, 2, 3), `kept = dp[1] + 1 = 2`, so `dp[3] = 3` and `best = 3`.
- `5`: no neighbours, so chains of length 1.

The answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for sorting; each element then does O(1) map work.
- Space: O(n) for the map.

## Pitfalls

- Read both `dp[num]` and `dp[num - 1]` before writing; updating `dp[num]` first would let one element count as both `num` and `num + 1`.
- Duplicates do not extend a run by themselves (`[1, 1, 2, 3]` is not consecutive), but one copy kept and one raised can.
- A raised value may exceed the input range (`10^6 + 1`); a map handles that without bounds checks.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp` | value `v` to the longest chain of distinct consecutive values ending at `v` |
| `num` | current element, in sorted order |
| `raised` | chain length if `num` is raised to `num + 1` |
| `kept` | chain length if `num` stays as `num` |
| `best` | longest chain seen |

narration.2: Sort so every chain an element can extend is built before the element arrives.
narration.3: dp maps a value to the longest chain of distinct consecutive values ending there.
narration.4: best is the longest chain found so far.
narration.5: Process the elements from smallest to largest.
narration.6: Raising num to num + 1 extends the best chain that ends at num.
narration.7: Keeping num extends the best chain that ends at num - 1.
narration.8: Record the raised option as a chain ending at num + 1, keeping any longer one already there.
narration.9: Record the kept option as a chain ending at num; both options were read first, so this element is not used twice.
narration.10: Update the overall best with both options.
narration.12: Return the longest chain of consecutive values.
